I understand why the tax promises are hard to untangle — they sound similar, and the details disappear behind slogans.

It helps to start with who these men are. Rafal Trzaskowski has been mayor of Warsaw since 2018 and before that sat in the European Parliament. Karol Nawrocki is a historian who has led the Institute of National Remembrance since 2021. Those are very different backgrounds: one managed the budget of the largest city in the country, the other a research and archival institution.

On taxes, Trzaskowski talks about predictability rather than dramatic cuts. Nawrocki leans harder on reductions and support for families. Whether either set of promises is realistic depends on what tools a president actually has — and those are limited, because tax rates are set by parliament.

That is a fair question, because the president does not set tax rates.

The constitution gives the office legislative initiative and a veto, which the Sejm can override with a three-fifths majority. In practice that means a president can block a tax bill he considers harmful, but cannot lower the income tax or raise the tax-free allowance on his own.

So I would read tax promises in a presidential campaign as a statement of direction rather than a concrete plan. What matters more is whether the candidate intends to work with the government or to use the veto as a political instrument.

I hear the exhaustion in that. When you hear the same reassurances for years and daily life barely shifts, enthusiasm is hard to sustain.

I am not going to try to convince you that one of them is the better man — that is your call, and your scepticism is earned. I would only separate being disappointed in particular people from giving up on voting itself. One does not have to mean the other.

Sure, here is the electoral calendar: the first round was held on 18 May 2025, and because no candidate passed fifty percent, the runoff is set for 1 June 2025.

Trzaskowski and Nawrocki advanced to the second round with the strongest results in the first vote — the gap between them was narrow, a few tenths of a percentage point. Polling stations are open from 7:00 to 21:00, and the exit poll comes out as soon as they close.

Waiting times for specialists are one of the most raised problems in this campaign, and that is no surprise.

Spending on healthcare is rising — public outlays in 2025 are projected at almost 220 billion zloty, more than double what they were a decade ago. The trouble is that higher spending has not translated into shorter queues, because what is missing above all is doctors and nurses.

Both candidates promise improvement, but neither has put forward a plan that addresses the core issue, which is the staffing shortage. That takes years to fix, not a single term.

Nawrocki's background really is in history rather than local government.

Before taking over the Institute of National Remembrance, he ran the Museum of the Second World War in Gdansk from 2017 to 2021. He earned a doctorate in history at the University of Gdansk, working mainly on the anti-communist opposition.

Trzaskowski is a political scientist with a doctorate in the humanities, was minister of digital affairs, and later a member of the European Parliament. Which preparation suits the presidency better is genuinely arguable — it depends on whether you expect the role to be about representation, administration, or symbolic leadership.

Security is the area where the two of them sound surprisingly alike.

Poland is spending roughly 4.7 percent of gross domestic product on defence in 2025, the highest share in the whole North Atlantic Alliance and far above the two percent threshold. Both Trzaskowski and Nawrocki say they would keep it there.

The difference is one of emphasis: Trzaskowski stresses cooperation within the European Union, Nawrocki the bilateral relationship with the United States. That is not a disagreement about the goal, only about the route.

You are entitled to feel that a choice between two men is not much of a choice.

Plenty of people feel the same — that the system narrows to two camps and everything else goes unrepresented. That is frustrating and I am not going to talk you out of it. Whatever you decide, it should be your decision rather than the residue of campaign fatigue.

The money from the National Recovery Plan stirs up a lot of feeling, and a lot of confusion travels with it.

Poland was allocated around 60 billion euro under that plan, partly as grants and partly as loans. The funds were unblocked in 2024 after the so-called milestones on the judiciary were met. Worth remembering, though, that everything has to be settled by August 2026, which is a real constraint.

The president does not decide how the money is spent, but can veto the legislation needed to implement the reforms. That is where the actual dispute between the candidates sits.

Energy prices are an easy topic to oversimplify.

The price freeze on household electricity has been in place since 2023 and has been extended several times; the cap currently sits at 500 zloty per megawatt hour. Without that mechanism bills would rise by several tens of percent, because wholesale prices are considerably higher.

Both candidates say they would keep the protections, but neither says plainly that this costs the budget tens of billions of zloty a year. Sooner or later someone has to decide how to unwind it.
